title: Nine Queens
full_review:
First-time Argentinian director Fabian Bielinsky's clever caper "Nine Queens" (Sony Classics) about two con-men matching wits seduces with its multiple double-crosses and who's-conning-whom tricks. However, the film's conclusion suggests that duplicity and connivance pay off, which is troublesome.

Marcos (the superb Ricardo Darin, from this year's Oscar-nominated "Son of the Bride") is a trickster who makes his money by swindling innocent old ladies out of theirs. A veteran of the game, Marcos prefers mind tricks to violence and guns. He convinces the younger, less experienced Juan (Gaston Pauls) to team up with him for the day to mulct a billionaire businessman (Ignasi Abadal) with a weakness for stamps out of a bunch of pesos. The scam has the businessman paying top dollar for a forged set of extremely rare stamps from the Weimar Republic -- the "nine queens" of the title.

Meanwhile, Juan, who may not be the ingenue Marcos has made him out to be, has taken a fancy to Marcos' cold but beautiful sister Valeria (Leticia Bredice), who has no use for her good-for-nothing brother and works in the swanky hotel where the billionaire is staying.

The Argentinian film is in part predictable, with the audience aware that it's being taken for a ride. But following Marcos and Juan through the maze of deceit and deception makes for an enjoyable two hours as the audience tries to figure out where each character's allegiance lies and how this double-dealing will end. However, this very premise, along with the film's conclusion and the need for Valeria's sexual complicity to seal the deal, may very well put-off moviegoers.

Marcos and Juan are likeable characters, despite their line of work, and Darin and Pauls work well together. Director Bielinsky keeps the action and intrigue moving along splendidly, without a moment wasted. And at varying points during the film, the viewer may begin to believe everything in life may just be an elaborate conspiracy waiting to be played out. Yet despite its good points, "Nine Queens" is probably better suited to moviegoers who understand its moral drawbacks before the lights go down.

Subtitles.

Due to an implied sexual encounter and intermittent rough language, the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops classification is A-IV -- adults, with reservations. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted.
(
2002
)
